hints: Look at the word each in the question, you need a trend that goes up every single step from Na to S with no dips or plateaus.

List the highest oxides you know: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, $\text{SO}_3$ and work out the oxidation number of the Period 3 element in each.
Now test the other ideas for a steady rise, does melting point rise all the way to sulfur, and do chloride solutions become more or less acidic across the period?
walkthrough:
**Recall the Period 3 elements in order**

Think of them side by side: Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S. We are looking for a property that gets bigger at every step.

This means even one fall or flat spot rules an option out.

**Check the highest oxidation number in the oxides**

Oxygen is almost always -2, so the highest oxide uses all the outer shell electrons for bonding.

$$\text{Na}_2\text{O} (+1), \text{MgO} (+2), \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 (+3), \text{SiO}_2 (+4), \text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} (+5), \text{SO}_3 (+6)$$

**See the perfect +1 pattern**

The oxidation number rises by exactly one each time, matching the group number from Group 1 to Group 16. This is because each successive element has one more valence electron to share with oxygen.

That steady 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 increase fits the question perfectly.

options.A: Correct. The maximum oxidation number equals the number of outer shell electrons used in the highest oxide, so it increases steadily: Na(+1) to S(+6). This is a smooth, stepwise increase with no exceptions.
options.B: False. Melting point rises from Na to Si (Si has a giant covalent structure with the highest melting point) then falls sharply to P and S which are simple molecular. It does not increase for each successive element.
options.C: False. The number of occupied orbitals stays the same in places. Na and Mg both use 6 orbitals ($1s, 2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z, 3s$), and P and S both use 9 orbitals because the fourth 3p electron in S pairs up in an already occupied orbital.
options.D: False. The trend is opposite. $\text{NaCl}$ gives a neutral solution (pH 7), while $\text{MgCl}_2$, $\text{AlCl}_3$, $\text{SiCl}_4$ and others hydrolyse to give increasingly acidic solutions, so pH decreases across the period, not increases.
